hints: Focus on the total number of valence electrons in each molecule, as an odd total must leave one electron unpaired.
Count for NO: N brings 5 and O brings 6 for a total of 11, so it must be a radical with an unpaired electron.
Now count NO2 and NH3 the same way and see which totals are odd and which allow all electrons to pair up in bonds and lone pairs.
walkthrough:
**Use the odd-electron shortcut**

Think simply first. If the total number of valence electrons is odd, they cannot all pair up, so at least one must be unpaired.

Valence rule:
$$\text{total valence e}^- = \text{(valence e}^- \text{ on N)} + \text{(valence e}^- \text{ on other atoms)}$$

**Check 1, NO**

Nitrogen is in Group 15 so it contributes 5, oxygen in Group 16 contributes 6.

$$5 + 6 = 11 \text{ valence electrons (odd)}$$ 
With 11 electrons, one is left over. So $\text{NO}$ has an unpaired electron and is a free radical.

**Check 2, NO2**

Do the same count. N gives 5, each O gives 6.

$$5 + (2 \times 6) = 17 \text{ valence electrons (odd)}$$ 
Again odd, so $\text{NO}_2$ must also contain an unpaired electron. This is why it readily dimerises to $\text{N}_2\text{O}_4$.

**Check 3, NH3**

N gives 5, each H gives 1.

$$5 + (3 \times 1) = 8 \text{ valence electrons (even)}$$ 
These 8 electrons pair up perfectly as three N-H bonds (6 electrons) plus one lone pair on N (2 electrons). So $\text{NH}_3$ has no unpaired electrons.

**Conclude the combination**

Only 1 and 2 have unpaired electrons, while 3 does not. That matches the 1 and 2 only combination.

options.A: Incorrect. This would mean 1, 2 and 3 are all radicals. While NO and NO2 are correct, NH3 has 8 valence electrons fully paired in bonds and a lone pair, so it has no unpaired electron.
options.B: Correct. Both NO with 11 valence electrons and NO2 with 17 valence electrons have odd electron counts and therefore contain one unpaired electron. NH3 with 8 valence electrons is fully paired.
options.C: Incorrect. This would mean 2 and 3 only are radicals. NO2 is correct, but NH3 is not a radical, and this choice wrongly leaves out NO which definitely has an unpaired electron.
options.D: Incorrect. This would mean 1 only is a radical. NO is indeed a radical, but this misses NO2 which also has an odd total of 17 valence electrons and an unpaired electron.
